item.title: The Smile that Hides Repressed Anger
item.description:
Sometimes anger can convince people that it’s not there. It doesn’t always come with a loud voice in a heated moment. It can roll in quietly, disguised as a tight jaw, sudden irritability, or a withdrawn spirit. Repressed anger is a deceptive emotion that many people carry.

By the time it’s recognized, it’s been living under the surface for months, and it no longer feels like anger. It has been shaping decisions and relationships for months or even years in ways that are hard to trace back to the source. Scripture has clear guidelines on anger:

In your anger do not sin: Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry. – Ephesians 4:26, NIV

The Bible tells us that we will experience anger, but it’s what we do in that anger that creates the struggles and issues. Repressed anger is deeper than a spiritual choice. Managing anger by keeping it out of sight and holding it at a distance can be the underlying assumption in faith communities. But now we are coming to understand that this is not handling it well and that the hidden anger carries real weight.

What Repressed Anger Really Looks Like

Repressed anger doesn’t identify itself by a name. It tends to present as persistent, low-grade sadness or unexplained irritability. It could be a withdrawal from once meaningful relationships.

This surfaces when people have spent years managing emotional responses for the sake of others, leading them to lose touch with what they’re actually feeling beneath the surface. By the time the anger surfaces, it may have been buried so long that the person no longer recognizes it for what it is.

Each individual has a choice to establish internal honesty. It’s not comfortable, but it is necessary for understanding how we manage emotional responses. In places that feel complicated or unflattering, an individual can begin to know themselves fully. Faith communities tend to suggest that certain emotions make self-examination a spiritual risk.

When individuals or communities have framed anger as a sign of spiritual immaturity or something that a truly trusting person doesn’t experience, honesty becomes difficult to access. Just because an emotion isn’t acknowledged doesn’t mean it disappears. It just learns to live quietly until it can’t anymore.

Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts. See if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting. – Psalm 139:23-24, NIV

The Hidden Cost of Keeping the Peace

Sometimes peace is a cover for avoidance, wearing a spiritual name. This happens when it involves staying quiet even though something genuinely needs to be said or moving past a wound before it has been addressed honestly. Surface-level peacemaking results in something that looks like patience but functions like suppression. The result is a calm exterior that pushes down everything that’s never been allowed to be named.

Anger does not have to be dissolved before it is examined to show emotional maturity. Wisdom in handling emotions comes from understanding the difference between unrestrained anger and engaging with what has been building beneath the surface.

Christian counselors help individuals who have chosen suppression over engagement, or who have lived under the belief that burying difficult emotions was the faithful choice. The process of understanding repressed anger begins with realizing that it does not protect a person. It only delays what will need to be addressed at a greater cost.

Repressed Anger and the Body’s Honest Response

Emotional suppression and physical health have a well-documented connection, especially when it comes to anger. The body will respond over time when anger has been withheld rather than processed. It shows up in chronic muscle tension, recurring headaches, digestive difficulties, and disrupted sleep.

The body was not created to absorb what the mind refuses to examine. It will register what is carried and communicate it in ways that become increasingly hard to ignore as the body reveals hidden issues through outward symptoms.

God’s Word offers straightforward instruction to be slow to anger, but there is a deeper meaning in this instruction than first appears. When an individual is slowed to anger, they adopt a posture that reflects thoughtfulness, reflection, and a willingness to listen before reacting. This is the opposite of suppression, which bypasses reflection entirely and buries the emotion without engagement.

Christian counselors can help individuals focus on the intersection of faith and emotional health by helping clients distinguish between the responses of suppression and reflection. Suppression is not being slow to anger. It is avoidance. Whatever an individual consistently avoids will find other ways to make itself known, whether through physical symptoms, relationships, or behavior.

My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry, because human anger does not produce the righteousness that God desires. – James 1:19-20, NIV

Finding Honest Ground Between Repressed Anger and Real Healing

When an individual moves away from the belief that their emotions are a spiritual problem and toward the understanding that the emotions carry spiritual information, they experience a meaningful shift. Anger often points to something real, even when it is buried. It indicates there was a boundary that was crossed, a wound that was minimized by others, or a loss that was never fully grieved.

Christian counselors recognize this shift and can help individuals name and grapple with the repressed anger that leads to an honest foundation where true healing can take place. Jesus never suggested that an offense be minimized or set aside.

He named it in a way that extends beyond interpersonal conflict. It reaches into the inner work of honestly acknowledging what has been dismissed or left untouched. Reconciliation requires honesty, whether it’s with oneself or with others.

The resolve to deal with what has been left unresolved isn’t a detour from faith, but rather wisdom in action. Many individuals find that their faith comes alive and is practical when they are honest about the repressed anger hidden beneath the surface.

Discover the Peace You Long For

People often smile when they don’t have the language or feel safe enough to do anything else. A smile is intended to be a reflection of wholeness that comes from the outward and inward life aligning. God’s Word does not ask people to perform emotionally. He invites them to genuine peace formed through honest engagement with Him in the reality of personal experience. This includes the parts that have been living quietly beneath the surface.

Jesus describes a peace that is not built on suppressing what is difficult, or on pretending that it’s not there. This peace comes to those who fully acknowledge what they carry. Those who are moving through the process of naming a long-buried emotion and following it to its source move into a place of honest healing. This isn’t a deficit of faith or the lack of it, but it can be how faith comes alive from the inside out.

Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled and do not be afraid. – John 14:27, NIV

If you think you may struggle with repressed anger, you don’t have to suppress it any longer. You don’t have to navigate the journey of understanding that anger alone. Contact our office and speak with our reception team to make an appointment. They will connect you with support that will help you navigate mental health and faith honestly.

item.title: Infidelity: How It Feels to Be Cheated On
item.description:
If you’ve experienced infidelity in your marriage, you’re not alone. According to Wendy Wang, Director of Research at the Institute of Family Studies, 20% of men and 13% of women in the United States have cheated on their spouse. That’s a fairly high number.

When you account for the fact that this study only focused on married couples, not those in long-term relationships, the number is likely higher. Add to that people who’ve had non-sexual affairs, such as those who have engaged in online or emotional affairs, and the number grows.

To say that you’re not alone if you’ve been cheated on is not an understatement. And while these numbers are staggering and indicate a larger, broader spiritual and moral problem in our modern world, knowing that you’re not experiencing this on your own can be comforting. What do they say about misery loving company?

Of course, being part of a statistic is not particularly comforting, especially when that statistic represents a broken relationship. But knowing that others before you have gone through this very thing and have made it out in one, thriving piece should bring some comfort.

If you’re reading this and have experienced infidelity, you might be feeling a whole host of uncomfortable emotions and be grappling with how to communicate them to others. Or maybe you’re the one who strayed, and you can’t quite figure out why your spouse is reacting the way they are. Many people know the technical reasons affairs hurt.

The broken promises and the betrayals are there, but beyond those cognitive reasons lies a broken, beating heart. Those emotions, the feelings and fallout of an affair, are not quite as easy to understand or communicate as the concrete broken rules. Keep reading to discover how being cheated on really feels.

Your comfort is gone.

If you’ve been in a relationship for any length of time, it’s logical to think that your partner is the person you go to for comfort. They represent unconditional love and are reaching for mutual goals with you, so it’s entirely natural to gravitate to this person when you need comfort or are dealing with any failure or disappointment.

When that person, your person, betrays you, that feeling of unconditional acceptance and love goes away. And because you no longer feel universally accepted by them, it’s infinitely more difficult to be vulnerable with them. So, instead of being transparent and raw with your partner, suddenly you have to be guarded.

You have to wonder if the news you’re about to share or the emotional breakdown that you’re on the verge of will be just one more thing that drives them away from you and into the arms of another. And to make matters worse, in the case of an affair, the person you usually go to for comfort is the very person who is causing you pain. That’s a difficult dynamic for your brain to understand and your heart to accept.

You don’t know who you are.

Couples tend to think of themselves as a unit. The “I” becomes “we” after you say, “I do,” and in many cases, long before that. Invitations are extended to you as a couple, and even your bank knows you as a unit. When one half of this singularity breaks the unity, you are left to identify as an individual again.

This is not to say that you’re automatically divorcing your spouse because of an affair, but this parting of the “we” in lieu of the “I” happens on an emotional level, long before divorce papers are ever served.

The point of marriage is to blend lives. Even the Bible tells us to become “one” with our spouse (Mark 10:6-9) and to abandon our singleness and, in some ways, the life we had prior to marriage. So, when something happens that loosens the glue that binds you together, you’re left with an identity crisis. “Who am I without them?” you might ask.

Blended lives are a beautiful thing, but when they fracture apart, the two individuals may find it more difficult to stand on their own than they did prior to the marriage.

You feel awkward.

Walking back into public life after an affair is a disorienting and awkward experience. You’re used to entering places in tandem and making decisions with the input of a partner. But now, you’re left to walk out into the world as a single. It shouldn’t be scary, right? You’ve done this before you were ever married. It shouldn’t be hard to be single again.

But you’re not the same young, somewhat naïve person you once were. You may not have the same youthful good looks or innocent charm to rely on that you once had, but you’re still you, whatever that means. You walk out into the world again, only this time, your confidence has been shaken, and you can’t seem to loosen this skepticism you feel that you will ever find anyone who thinks you’re worthy of love again.

You think that every eye is on you, whether they are judging, wondering, or even sympathizing. If you’ve been the victim of infidelity, you wonder if everyone knows, as if you’re wearing a scarlet letter on your sleeve.

You wonder if anyone finds you attractive or whether they ever will. After all, you’re older now, and those cute little glances and shy smiles you used to flash at prospective suitors don’t have the same effect. You wish that trick still worked on your spouse. You love them still, but you’re wondering if they love you.

Awkwardness and the self-awareness of your awkwardness can be overwhelming, not just to your mind, but also to your body. Your cheeks redden, and your heart begins to race, and you haven’t even gotten out of the car yet.

When you don’t know who you are and don’t particularly like what you think you are, it’s much more difficult to walk your daily life. Unfortunately, feeling awkward often leads to less than confident behavior, which might produce less than positive or enthusiastic responses from others. This then becomes a cycle where your fear of being awkward actually makes you, well, awkward.

Breaking Free

All these feelings that bloom out of infidelity can be overwhelming. They might feel as if they are permanent, that the damage is irreversible, and that you will never feel like yourself again. The good news is that infidelity, like every other human condition, is not too big or ominous for your Heavenly Father.

Through the power of the Holy Spirit, you can find that peace again. You can learn to trust and to feel confident, not because of the love and attention of a partner, but because you are a child of God. You can live a life that is full of joy and fulfillment, whether that means that you’re married or not. And perhaps most importantly, you can learn to forgive.

By laying out your heart to the Lord, reading Scripture, and seeking His face, you can find a path out of the insecurities and scars of infidelity into a new, more confident place. Maybe that means reconciling with your spouse. Maybe it means moving on in a different direction. God knows what’s best for you, and He wants to lead you to it.

Part of that healing process might include the guidance of a Christian therapist. A therapist can help you reconcile your feelings of betrayal and frame them in a way that you understand. They can help you learn to express yourself by giving you vocabulary and prompts that help you articulate your feelings, process them, and eventually move on from them.

A New Life

Infidelity doesn’t have to mean the end of your marriage, and certainly not the end of your life. You can recover from the battle scars of betrayal. You can forgive. You can reconcile. But you can also move on to a new life filled with possibilities and purpose.

It might be difficult to express or even understand the deep emotions you’re feeling right now, but with time, God’s guidance, and perhaps time with a professional counselor, you can start moving out of the fog and back into the light of God. Soon you will be walking confidently into the world, whether that’s alone or in a healed relationship.

item.title: Is It Possible for Kids to Control their Emotions? A Child Therapist Weighs In
item.description:
Upon asking if it is possible for kids to control their emotions, it is equally important to ask whether it is reasonable to expect it. As a therapist who has worked with children five years old and older, I will answer yes to both questions. Yes, it is possible for kids to control their emotions. And yes, it is reasonable to expect a child five years old to be able to control their emotions.

However, defining what that control means and looks like is key to understanding how it will look in operation and function in a child. Controlling emotions refers to the ability to identify, steward, and respond to emotional stimulation in a balanced or healthy way versus dismissing or ignoring them. Controlling emotions in therapeutic terms is referred to as emotional regulation.

Emotional regulation is the process of managing the intensity, duration, and expression of emotions to respond correctly to situations while maintaining mental well-being. Note that this definition does not intend for the child to avoid or repress the feelings that arise but requires them to manage their emotional reaction.

Emotional reaction management helps ensure that decision-making does not become overwhelmed and that social interactions remain mostly positive.

Every Child Can Learn About Emotions

Per the National Center for Education Statistics, children can learn more about their emotions than we sometimes give them credit for. Even young children are taking in information, remembering patterns, and beginning to connect what they feel with what is happening around them. By ages 2-3, children can begin holding on to information in meaningful ways.

As they move closer to ages 4-5, their memory, attention, and ability to follow simple steps continue to grow. This matters because emotional regulation is also learned step by step. A child may not always respond perfectly, but with consistent teaching, modeling, and practice, they can learn to pause, name what they feel, and choose a safer or more appropriate response.

Teaching children emotional regulation requires teaching them in a way they can comprehend. Children need the concept of “emotional regulation” broken down into a more understandable construct such as “pause and check in.” Often, taking the foundational meaning of words and using them with a younger mind helps them better connect with meaning.

Emotional regulation at its foundation is all about pausing and checking in with yourself first. Although emotional regulation is profoundly serious, allowing a child to learn emotional regulation by making it into a “tag-your-it” type of game is okay.

As a therapist who has worked with children and adolescents, the intensity can be lessened if fun can be had. However, always remind the child that fun is okay, and safety is the best friend of fun. We can have fun if you are safe, and so is everyone else. This is layered, but it is the step-by-step method that was previously mentioned. Once you convey the concept, begin to build on it to add other important ideas regarding emotional regulation.

What A Child Needs to Know About Their Emotions

The first thing that a child needs to know about their emotions is that they are not bad, stupid, make them an annoying person, make them weird, should make them feel scared, or any other negative conclusion they may have come to.

Children must know that emotions are a part of their human experience and their emotions are God given. The goal is to help them not only regulate their emotions but to understand them so that they can avoid shame or even embarrassment because of what they are feeling.

Here are a few simple phrases that can help children and adolescents feel seen, supported, and less alone in what they are experiencing.

  • “It’s okay to not feel okay.” – Normalizes odd feelings without judgement.
  • “Sadness can feel lonely. Can I sit with you quietly?” – Normalize maintaining connecting during tough times versus isolation.
  • “Crying is okay. I will get you some tissue.” – The focus is getting the child comfortable with being supported while being validated (seen).
  • “Feeling scared is hard. What do you need right now? – The focus is getting the child to speak to how to name what would meet their need, by using their words.

The key is to keep it simple, continue step-by-step and to model. Children need to see that we not only understand but are present. Being present is not just about our bodies being in the same space, meaning proximity. They need to know that an adult is present in their eyes and with their hearts. This matters to any child in any emotional state at any time.

Modeling is one of the most effective ways children learn emotional regulation. Children are always watching how the adults around them respond to frustration, sadness, disappointment, fear, and even joy.

When adults can slow down, name what is happening, and respond steadily, children begin to learn that emotions can be felt without taking over the whole moment. This is not about being perfect in front of a child. It is about allowing the child to see regulation practiced in real time.

One Step Further

The goal is to build a foundation of understanding not only emotional regulation but to also take it one step further to begin establishing good mental health. Think about that for a second, what if it was widespread practice to put into place the building blocks for children to have a good headstart to sound mental health.

Children who understand their emotions grow into adults who understand their emotions as well as how to manage them. Children can control their emotions when they learn that their emotions are a part of their human experience.

As a therapist who is a Christian, I can tell you that unpacking that truth, along with the reality that God equipped us with emotions for a purpose, and that they are good. God speaks of emotions and how to manage them throughout His Word.

A child must know that anger is real and God is aware. Fear is going to show up; God knew it and warned us that we were going to have to stand up to fear, not run from it. With God’s help, they can emotionally regulate.

Children are easy to teach when we know what we are teaching and how to teach it. When controlling emotions is taught with consideration of self, others, environment, and outcome, it helps to create step-by-step instruction, which creates consistency in demonstration and modeling.

As children grow into adolescents the emotional lessons that they learn will undoubtedly stick with them while allowing additional knowledge of more complicated emotional concepts.

Sensitivity can be learned, and due to our culture, which is heavily packed with less-kind television programming, video games, and movie entertainment, sensitivity is an emotion we cannot afford to leave children to gather on their own.

Teaching children how to manage anger and express it in a healthy way is a necessity our current society can no longer ignore. Ignoring emotional health until it becomes a crisis. When a child is in mental crisis, there is less chance of helping them, and it is harder to assist the appointed adult with comprehending what is happening with them in the moment.

The more clarity that can be given to children to help them identify and understand their emotions, the better we can help them manage what they go through while continuing to understand who they are and will become emotionally.

item.title: Bible Verses for Overeating Disorder
item.description:
Is overeating a struggle for you? Many of us face this struggle daily in our abundant culture, where food is tempting and readily available. However, the Bible can help you have better health by reminding you to curb your overeating habits.

When you use specific verses of God’s Word to prepare yourself, you can fight back with confidence when you are tempted to overeat. Jesus used Scripture to fight temptation at a time when he was very hungry (Matt. 4:1-11). If he did this to overcome Satan, we can do the same thing to gain spiritual victory.

The following verses are powerful weapons for you to fight temptation. Meditate on them, memorize them, write them down, post them where you see them often, and save them to your phone. The more ways you hide God’s Word in your heart, the more easily you will remember it when you are tempted to overeat. You can ask the Holy Spirit to bring them to mind when you need accountability in your eating habits.

The Best Bible Verses for Overeating Disorder

You can turn each of the following verses into a prayer in times of temptation. God will meet you right in those moments and give you the strength to overcome. He promises to deliver you from whatever temptation you face, and he will empower you to make better choices for your health.

…the rules of the Lord are true, and righteous altogether. More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb. – Psalm 19:9b-10

God considers his laws to be more desirable than the sweetest food available during Bible times – honey. His laws are more desirable than the finest gold, or perhaps your food craving of choice: chips, French fries, doughnuts, ice cream, pizza, or whatever tempts you most.

Remember that when you follow God’s laws, you will be blessed with a clean conscience. You won’t be riddled with guilt and shame like you may be when you overeat. God will help you make wise eating choices so you can live a disciplined life for his Kingdom work. His laws lead to life, while our poor choices lead to destruction, so remember this verse when you are tempted.

So I will bless you as long as I live; in your name I will lift up my hands. My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips. – Psalm 63:4-5

What are the richest foods you have tasted? Steak, lobster, cheesecake, or something else? Are you honestly as satisfied with God as you are when you eat these rich foods? You can learn to be more satisfied with God’s presence than you are with food, though this will take discipline.

The peace you find in God’s presence lasts much longer than the pleasure you get from eating rich food. When you learn to gain your true satisfaction from God, your faith will be grounded even while food looks tempting to you.

Delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart. – Psalm 37:4

What are the desires of your heart when you are tempted to overeat? It’s probably not to simply feel full or enjoy the taste and texture of food. Most of us overeat to soothe our emotions and fill a place inside that feels empty. Often people with overeating disorders deal with loneliness, rejection, anxiety, depression, and other problems.

A caring Christian counselor can help you get to the roots of why you overeat. You can learn that taking delight in the Lord is much more satisfying than overeating, and you can trust him with the deepest desires of your heart.

How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! – Psalm 119:103

God’s Word will become sweeter to you the more you meditate on it, study it, and apply it to your life. The Bible has healing properties, just like real honey does. But God’s Word heals you with God’s love, comfort, encouragement, protection, and joy as you learn to relax in his presence and enjoy time with him. Each day, meet with God for a few minutes, asking him to make his words sweeter than honey to you and healing for your soul.

Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips! Do not let my heart incline to any evil, to busy myself with wicked deeds in company with men who work iniquity, and let me not eat of their delicacies! – Psalm 141:3-4

These verses address the issue of controlling what we say. But they can also apply to what food passes over our lips. We can ask God to stand guard over our lips when we are faced with a tempting situation.

He will help you stop putting things into your mouth that aren’t good for you. You can ask God to keep you from drifting toward evil choices and help you avoid the wrong kinds of delicacies. The next time you are tempted, simply pray “Guard my lips,” and God will be right beside you.

I cry to you, O Lord; I say, “You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.” – Psalm 142:5

When you feel like you want that third piece of cake or fourth slice of pizza, you can pray this verse. You can say, “Lord, I think I want this food right now. But I know my true craving should be for you because you alone can satisfy me.” Then walk away from the temptation, drink a glass of water, and engage in a different activity. God will be your refuge in that moment, a haven where you can find comfort that lasts longer than the food you are craving.

If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it. – Proverbs 25:16

The Bible is eminently practical. Any food, even healthy food like honey, can make you sick if you overeat. Choose to eat a balanced diet of nourishing foods to protect your health and feel your best. When you are tempted to overeat in certain food categories, remember this verse and don’t succumb to temptation.

Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” – Matthew 26:41

Our minds and spirits may be willing to make wise food choices, but the sinful nature of our flesh is vulnerable to temptation. All of us face this scenario at one time or another, particularly when we are stressed. But God will help you in the very moment of temptation if you cry out to him. Admit to him that your flesh is weak, and ask him to deliver you from the temptation to overeat.

No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation, he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it. – 1 Corinthians 10:13

This verse can be a practical comfort to you in times of temptation. Ask God to provide you a way out when you are about to overeat. He might instruct you to remove tempting foods from your pantry or eat a mini-meal before going to a restaurant. You can form more practical strategies to serve as escape routes with a qualified Christian counselor.

Christian Counseling for Overeating

The roots of overeating run deep for most people. You may need help from a Christian counselor to overcome overeating disorder. A counselor will offer Bible-based care with compassion and understanding. Your counselor will encourage you with principles that can keep you on track for a healthier lifestyle.

item.title: What is OCD and Do I Have It?
item.description:
Have you ever wondered, “What is OCD and do I have it?” Perhaps thoughts like these sound familiar: “Did I turn the stove off before I left for work?” “I need to make sure the locks are secure one last time or something bad will happen to my family.” “My hands feel dirty even after five times washing.” “If I don’t follow through with [this compulsion], I may be responsible for a loved one’s death.”

Do these or similar thoughts occupy your mind each day? Do you find yourself spending too much time ruminating on thoughts you didn’t choose to reflect on; thoughts you can’t seem to get out of your head? Are those thoughts often accompanied by behaviors others might consider bizarre or confusing?

These are just a few examples of the unsettling reality that obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) sufferers battle every day. This article will explore facts vs. common myths related to OCD, the different variations of this unique disorder, and what we can do about it.

What is OCD?

OCD is a unique disorder that has origins in anxiety but is given its own category due to its complex profile. OCD is often chronic, meaning managing it will likely be a constant battle, but with help and treatment, symptoms can decrease significantly, and sufferers can find hope!

As the name suggests, it is characterized by both obsessions and compulsions. The obsessions take the form of intrusive, unwanted, and disturbing thoughts that cause significant anxiety for the sufferer. Compulsions are then used to find temporary relief from these thoughts, offering the sufferer the feeling of control.

Unfortunately, when compulsions are carried out, this only increases the likelihood of intrusive thoughts recurring and strengthens the association between the thoughts, anxiety, and relief found in the behaviors. As with any uncomfortable feeling or situation, when avoidance strategies are employed, we only strengthen our brain’s association with the feared object, convincing our brain that it must be truly dangerous.

This creates a strong feedback loop, causing our brains to obsess over the anxiety-producing thought or event to keep us safe. Although the brain is doing its job, these obsessions can cause suffering, and so the brain finds ways to avoid the painful feelings through compulsive behaviors. Remember – avoidance increases anxiety symptoms. The most helpful way to reduce these uncomfortable experiences is to face them with the help of a trained professional.

Obsessions vs. Compulsions

Obsessions are preliminary to the compulsive behaviors individuals employ to alleviate discomfort. The person begins to ruminate on the intrusive thoughts, and significant amounts of time are spent worrying about the obsessions and practicing compulsions. Compulsions always come out of obsessions as a response to the discomfort they cause, though the link may appear subtle at times.

One thing to note about obsessions is they almost always manifest as an attack on something we deeply care about. This may be a faith belief, part of your character, someone you love, your health, and even your worth. These disturbing intrusive thoughts carry so much powerful weight because they strike to the heart of your deepest values and hidden fears.

Doubt is a common byproduct of the OCD experience, partly because these obsessions can lead you to doubt your morals, beliefs, reality, and even your humanity. But remember, the key thing to understand about obsessions is that they are intrusive – meaning unwanted. They are not a description of who you are or what you believe.

When intrusive thoughts wage war against your mind, the doubt and distress you have are evidence that these thoughts do not come from your character. They are not true beliefs or true moral dilemmas.

If we were to externalize intrusive thoughts and imagine them as a person, they would be manipulative, using your deepest-held values to create false allegations against you, using lies to confuse you and make you wonder whether your character ever had morals or integrity in the first place. And they would be doing all these things in the shadows, making you feel isolated and alone.

Hold on to your values and remember that intrusive thoughts are lies and they function like a bully. They don’t get to tell you who you are, and although at times it may not feel like it, they only hold as much power as you allow.

Common OCD Misconceptions

As with many mental health conditions, popular culture has created stereotypes that can increase confusion between the facts and the myths surrounding OCD. Many people will use the phrase “I’m so OCD” or “you are being OCD” to describe someone who tends toward perfectionism, values organization, or has challenges related to hypochondriasis or germophobia.

There is confusion about what OCD truly is, how the symptoms can present, and the severity of symptoms that lead to a diagnosis. Phrases and stereotypes like these can have a minimizing effect for those truly suffering with the condition.

The obsessional theme of organization and sanitization has gained popularity in recent years, leading many people to understand OCD from this one-dimensional frame. However, there are several different categories of obsessions, some of which may be surprising. If you wonder about OCD but don’t obsess about germs or organization, this list may interest you.

Common Obsessional Themes and Related Compulsions

This is a list of common OCD themes found in the DSM. This list is not exhaustive and, as with all mental health topics, everyone will experience the condition differently. Someone may only have one type of OCD; another person may struggle with several of these. These themes can change over time, and you may develop away from one obsession into new ones. There are also varying levels of severity that may change in different seasons of life.

Often, during high-stress seasons, OCD symptoms may flare, a common phenomenon shared by many disorders. Some themes of OCD obsessions include contamination, sexual, harm/violence, scrupulosity (religious), sensorimotor, and responsibility. Here we will provide a quick overview of each theme listed, but more information is available on trusted websites, such as the International OCD Foundation, for those who are interested in a deeper dive.

Contamination OCD is one of the more widely known subtypes because of its exposure in popular culture. People with this subtype of obsession are preoccupied with cleanliness and sanitation and excessively worry about becoming contaminated with illness or germs. A person may feel “dirty” until they can sanitize to a satisfactory level, sometimes at the risk of skin harm from excessive washing.

Some people may need to wash a certain number of times or practice compulsions until they “feel right.” Another common compulsion related to contamination OCD is rigid behavior around eating, and a highly controlled environment to avoid feeling contaminated.

Sexual OCD involves distressing thoughts related to sexual orientation or unwanted images. People with this subtype may experience shame related to mental images of performing inappropriate sexual acts or participating in sexual ways not acceptable to the individual. Another common theme in this subtype includes doubt about sexual orientation.

An individual may have doubts about their identity and where the thoughts and feelings come from. Common compulsions related to this subtype include reassurance seeking, mental avoidance of unwanted images and thoughts, or monitoring their reactions to the thoughts.

People experiencing Harm/Violence OCD often experience disturbing thoughts and images related to harming themself or a loved one. Additionally, thoughts related to fear of loved ones being hurt if compulsions are not performed are common.

Compulsions related to harm OCD include mental efforts to avoid distressing material, avoiding triggers, avoiding objects that could be used to cause harm, seeking reassurance, and mental checking of one’s character or morals. Sometimes, seemingly unrelated compulsions may include ensuring the right outfit is picked out, or other elements of the environment are under control to prevent the terrible end of a loved one that day.

Scrupulosity is a form of OCD that focuses on faith and religion. The scrupulous individual is consumed by the fear of offending God, sinning, or morally compromising their beliefs. Disturbing images related to sinful acts commonly coincide with this subtype.

Individuals may perform compulsions through ritualistic patterns, such as saying the “right” prayers, repeatedly asking for forgiveness, mental assessments of one’s character and morals, reassurance seeking, mental rationalizing to “argue” with the thoughts, and repeating Scripture a preset number of times, or until it “feels right.”

Elements of prayer, scripture memorization, and repentance can look like regular behaviors for someone practicing faith, but they become compulsions when they are done ritualistically in an effort to offset the discomfort from obsessions, rather than stemming from devoted practice. The individual may also practice their faith alongside the ritualistic compulsions. The difference is subtle, but important to recognize.

Sensorimotor (somatic) OCD includes obsessions related to bodily functions and feelings. Individuals may become hyper-aware of automatic body processes such as blinking, heartbeat, and breathing, and compulsions may include trying to take control over blinking and breathing through patterns and rigid rules related to the number of blinks or breaths in a given amount of time.

Individuals may spend large amounts of time monitoring somatic processes, avoiding situations that trigger hyper-awareness, and seeking reassurance and validation through research and questioning others’ experiences.

Responsibility OCD involves feelings of being responsible to prevent bad things from happening, or fears and doubts related to your behaviors causing a negative event. Those suffering from this subtype often feel responsible for the emotions of those around them and try to control the environment to prevent a negative outcome.

Though their intentions are noble, symptoms of responsibility OCD can quickly become consuming, causing significant distress to the sufferer and tension in social relationships. Efforts to control the environment can overtake an individual’s time and energy, leaving little left over for necessary tasks, such as taking care of health, housekeeping, work, and social spheres.

Responsibility OCD can also coincide with memory OCD, where an individual may doubt their memories or believe they have forgotten something important. Those suffering from this subtype may believe they hit someone with their car or were responsible for a negative situation although there is no proof of it ever occurring. These individuals seek reassurance and compulsively check for evidence to relieve the doubts about their memories.

How do I know if it’s an obsession?

We all have intrusive thoughts sometimes – those thought darts that seem to come out of nowhere and attack our innermost value systems. The experience can be alarming, but individuals without OCD can move on and not become consumed by the thought. OCD obsessions are different because they become consuming. They are distressing, often disturbing thoughts that feel like an onslaught the sufferer cannot prevent.

Obsessions take up time and mental space, and lead to compulsions to alleviate the pain these intrusive thoughts are causing. Although compulsions can be ritualistic, time-consuming, and energy-draining, many individuals battling OCD find comfort in the control that compulsions offer, and in the temporary relief from anxiety. Unfortunately, the anxiety comes back quickly when the intrusive thoughts return, making the association with fear stronger.

The Reassurance Feedback Loop

Seeking and receiving reassurance from anxiety can be a helpful way to connect with a trusted friend, validate your feelings, or gain a new perspective. However, reassurance seeking can become a compulsion when it is done continually and with an attempt to relieve anxieties and doubts generated from OCD obsessions.

Just like with any other compulsion, the association between relief from anxiety and reassurance seeking can be powerful, leading to a rigid pattern of behavior. Seeking reassurance can become a trap when an individual can no longer trust their own thoughts and may even feel like they cannot trust their reality without the input of another.

It can become a form of dependence when we continually seek validation from others to find relief. It is important to learn tools that bolster your inner strengths and aid in overcoming doubts without needing reassurance from others. Freedom from the reassurance feedback loop can increase autonomy and the quality of your relationships.

Put your mind at ease

Remember, OCD obsessions often target our most cherished beliefs and values. If you are having uncomfortable intrusive thoughts and are wondering whether they inform your character, remind yourself that these thoughts are unwanted and direct contradictions to your inner value set.

They do not come from a hidden desire, and your feelings of anxiety or disgust related to these thoughts are evidence of this discrepancy. Don’t let OCD’s manipulations fool you. If you are distressed by the obsessions trying to take over your mind, you can find comfort remembering these intrusive thoughts are evidence of the very values they are trying to attack.

Consider counseling

In counseling, you can explore OCD symptoms and how they affect your life. Your counselor will help you add tools that can equip you for battling and overcoming obsessions and compulsions. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Behavioral Therapy are two of the most common treatments that offer relief from OCD symptoms.

Many individuals also find relief through medication. Through counseling, you can find the support and training needed to find freedom from compulsions and minimize the impact of obsessions on your life. Suffering in silence can increase OCD’s power.

Although it can be uncomfortable or feel embarrassing to openly discuss and dissect OCD obsessions and compulsions with someone, you can find significant relief in shifting the power dynamic away from the OCD.

Conclusion

Obsessive-compulsive disorder is an exhausting condition that causes great distress and can become debilitating when left untreated. Individuals may feel trapped by OCD obsessions and compulsions and consumed by the amount of time and mental effort exerted through simply trying to make it through the day.

Unfortunately, most of the time, compulsive efforts to relieve the discomfort created by OCD obsessions only reinforce the cycle and can make the distress and obsessions stronger. Counseling can help sufferers find relief, valuable education, and new tools to manage OCD symptoms and reduce their impact on your life.

Although OCD is most often a chronic condition, you can find great relief by developing insight and skills to battle obsessions and compulsions. Consider reaching out to our team today to find a counselor and begin your journey of discovery and renewed freedom.

And always remember – self-compassion goes a long way when learning new skills! No one is going to get it perfect, and that is okay. It is important to offer yourself grace when working toward new goals.

item.title: Faith and Healing for the Emotionally Unavailable Heart
item.description:
Some relationships look fine on the surface, but something essential is missing on the inside. The conversations happen, and plans are made, but life keeps moving, and the emotional connection that should anchor it feels out of reach.

It could be a partner, a parent, or an emotionally unavailable sibling, leaving a person questioning their worth, their perception, and their faith. The desire to be truly known and to matter to someone is not something to be considered prideful. It is, in fact, a human desire for genuine connection that has been wired into us from the beginning.

God created us with this desire, so He understands when it goes awry and something is missing. For individuals to understand that they must take an honest look at what lies beneath the surface, they often find that the experience involves more than just feeling lonely in a relationship.

Sometimes it is a deeper reckoning with their own emotional needs and a question of whether those needs are valid. This is a difficult thought to process, but it can be the beginning of something meaningful and lasting.

What It Means to Be Emotionally Unavailable

There is a pattern that goes beyond being reserved. It describes a consistent inability or unwillingness to engage in purposeful, emotionally deep conversations within close relationships. Individuals can be physically present and dependent in practical ways, while at the same time being emotionally distant and avoiding vulnerable conversations and deflecting personal topics.

They will maintain surface-level engagement, keeping others at arm’s length. This pattern indicates that some individuals have difficulty expressing feelings and are uncomfortable with intimacy.

The complexity of the situation is that the person is not always aware of what they are doing. Often, the pattern develops gradually as a way of navigating environments where emotional expression is not safe. It is frequently observed that the person learned at a young age to keep things internal so they would be manageable. This became the default, and these are rarely examined until something in life forces the question.

There is a connection in Scripture between the interior life and the health of everything that flows from it. By watching over the heart with diligence and individual will, one will find that life flows much more easily. (Proverbs 4:23)

How Emotional Walls Develop Over Time

The walls individuals build are not always deliberate. Most of the time, these are built in response to an experience, such as rejection, abandonment, or unprocessed grief, that has taught a person it is safer to close off than to stay open.

It has been noted that attachment wounds formed in early relationships shape how adults engage emotionally later in life. Those who have had emotional expression met with ridicule, silence, or dismissal in their younger years develop a natural tendency to stop expressing any emotion. It is a protective instinct that yields a habit that will linger long after the threat has passed.

People often absorb narratives about emotional strength that can influence how they define emotional stability. For these individuals, the idea that vulnerability is weakness or that needing others is a liability leads them to create a relational armor that is difficult to remove.

Christian counselors work with individuals who carry these narratives without naming them. They help the individual recognize that the armor once served a purpose but is no longer needed. This recognition can create a pivotal shift in the healing process.

The shift from guarded and closed to something open and live is a promise found in the Old Testament. God promises to give us a new heart and a new spirit as He removes the heart of stone from our flesh. (Ezekiel 36:26)

Loving Someone Who Is Emotionally Unavailable

Caring deeply for someone unable to meet the same emotional depth can be a disorienting experience. There are patterns of needs getting adjusted downward, silence is interpreted as rejection, and the desire for closeness feels like an unreasonable demand.

When individuals navigate this kind of relational dynamic, they realize the complexity and how it does not follow a simple set of rules. These dynamics require that compassion and self-protection coexist. It will also emphasize that patient, honest boundaries are necessary as they explore the difference between someone unwilling to engage emotionally and someone who does not know how to.

A healthy relationship requires the person doing the loving to stay grounded in their own emotional reality. It has been noted that, over time, unreciprocated emotional bids can erode a person’s sense of self-worth and make that person feel invisible in the relationship.

Reaching out to a Christian counselor provides a way to find much-needed clarity about what is healthy to sustain healthy relationships and what changes may be possible. It also opens up the possibilities of firm boundaries that need to be established to protect both individuals.

Finding Wholeness Through Faith and Support

The process of healing from emotional disconnection, whether the pattern is one’s own or shaped by years of relationships, benefits from both professional care and spiritual grounding. God consistently points to a promise of wholeness, as He sees what is hidden and invites the wounded into genuine restoration. This is an invitation that extends to the emotional life as much as it does the spiritual life, and these two are rarely as separate as they may seem.

Psychotherapy focuses on attachment patterns, emotional regulation, and relational history, which shows measurable progress for individuals dealing with emotional disconnection. But when faith-informed care becomes integrated into the process, there is a space of creativity, where the whole person and not just symptoms or behaviors are addressed.

Christian counselors who are familiar with this integrated framework understand that emotional healing and spiritual formation can move together. Individuals often find that as they are willing to open one door, the other opens with it.

There is a promise found in Scripture that is not found in a clinical framework alone. It is the invitation given by Jesus in the book of Matthew:

Come to Me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest. – Matthew 11:28, NASB

Healing Begins

Emotional unavailability doesn’t have to be the final word on a relationship. For individuals who have spent years behind walls they didn’t consciously choose to build, and those who have loved someone through those walls, healing is real and reachable. It will require honesty, patience, and the decision to intentionally look beneath the surface at what remains to be addressed. This journey toward emotional wholeness is not linear, and it doesn’t have to be walked alone.

Just as God fashioned the human heart for intimacy, He also restores what has been locked away. Even though it might feel permanently closed, it is not beyond His reach. You can choose to reopen the heart as a movement toward maturity and an honest decision to release what the past has held, and be willing to step into what the future will hold.

This is an assurance that belongs to every individual who has walked through emotional distance. Whether it was the one living behind the wall or the one waiting at its edge, there is a promise that God sees both sides.

For I know the plans that I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for calamity to give you a future and a hope. – Jeremiah 29:11, NASB

If you find yourself navigating the weight of an emotionally distant relationship, regardless of what side of the wall you are on, you do not have to walk that journey alone. Our reception team can connect you with a counselor who understands the emotional and spiritual dimensions of that dynamic. One phone call can help you start your journey toward tearing down the wall that you never meant to build.

item.title: What to Do When Your Partner Is Showing Signs of Abandonment Issues
item.description:
Relationships can be tricky even at the best of times. This is true for romantic, platonic, or family relationships. Many of the most frustrating behaviors in relationships can be signs of abandonment issues, and signals that the person you’re trying to love has past hurt inside of them. If you can find the balance of giving grace to people while building healthier boundaries, even the most insecure of relationships will have a fighting chance to flourish.

The Pattern of Abandonment

Maybe your new relationship started great, but now they’re acting weird, and you’re wondering what shifted. Perhaps that new friend with whom you clicked so well at first has recently started getting clingy and annoying. It has become an issue, and maybe you would cut them off if you didn’t feel so bad about doing that.

For example, maybe you want to build a healthier relationship with your mother, but you’ve realized that means you will have to call her out on a few things. It might help if you understood how her abandonment issues affected her parenting style, and by default, you.

Abandonment trauma breeds cycles of behavior where one damaged person neglects or rejects those closest to them. They, in turn, pass the damage onto others. This can lead to walking out on meaningful relationships without closure, or squeezing the life out of relationships because they’re afraid of being abandoned.

This pattern continues until someone sees the signs of abandonment issues and intervenes. No one is doomed to repeat the past or live as a victim of it. It takes work, gentleness, and wisdom to change course.

We can’t fix people, and we shouldn’t try. We can, however, be a better support for them, be patient with them, build better boundaries, and model healthier attachment in the way we treat them. In the process, we might realize signs of abandonment issues in our own lives and be forced to confront them. Sometimes, for us to love others better, we must work to resolve something in us that has been damaged for a long time.

Common Signs of Abandonment Issues in Relationships

Abandonment trauma and neglect go hand in hand. Many parents are loving and supportive only when they have time to be, but absent and emotionally distant the rest of the time. In this way, they are neglectful without realizing it, and cause abandonment trauma without meaning to.

This results in a person with abandonment trauma being constantly anxious about being left, ignored, or not cared for by the person they care for the most. This can lead to toxic behavior, and a lot of clear signs for those who can see them. Here are some signs to look for.

Things move quickly with them

You’ve just met them, and you don’t even know their middle name or birthday month, but they are already talking about the future. Not only is fast behavior like this disconcerting, but it is a sign of someone terrified of being forgotten and overlooked.

You might be guilty of this yourself. You may feel as if you are constantly holding yourself back from saying, “I love you,” or wanting to define the relationship. This is one of the clearest and most common signs of abandonment issues.

The person feeling this way needs to hear this: You have inherent worth and deserve to be seen, understood, and valued by others. Your experiences in the past of being overlooked and undervalued were unfair, and they caused significant damage. Now you must find your self-worth outside of the way that others treat you, whether they show you love or not.

You’re not “too much,” you’re not unlovable, and your desire to be loved is one of the most valid things. You must sit with these thoughts as often as possible, and let them into your soul as deeply as you can.

They panic over seemingly small things

People with abandonment trauma are overthinkers and worriers, sometimes to the extreme. A subtle shift in mood can cause them to panic, just as an unanswered text message can feel like a dreadful confirmation of someone’s disinterest.

Then they get stuck with another question: do they confront the issue even if it means they will come across as neurotic, or do they repress their anxiety even though it feels overwhelming? Either thing might result in being rejected and abandoned, just as they feared.

There are few things as painful as being undervalued, especially when it happens at a young age. People with abandonment trauma have determined that they are forgettable and that their needs are not a priority for anyone else. That’s an incredibly heavy thought. It’s no wonder that they are hyperaware of every shift and change in the relationship.

The way for them to break out of their anxiety and overthinking is to be reassured and to build their tolerance to discomfort. Be kind when they ask for reassurance because it probably took courage for them to speak up. Encourage them to sit with their discomfort as they wait for replies or question your mood, though. They need consistency and kindness, and they need to develop stronger methods of coping.

They’re either the first person to walk away or they remain in toxic relationships

One of the easiest ways to see signs of abandonment issues in people is to look at their previous relationships and identify any patterns of repeated behavior.

Perhaps they tend to stay in relationships where they are consistently treated poorly, used, and taken for granted. Maybe they always end the relationship before it’s had a chance to develop. The first person is more comfortable being alone, while the second is terrified of being alone, but both show clear signs of abandonment issues. Both of these people need to face their fears.

The person who is afraid of being alone needs to spend more time alone and to develop competence in caring for themselves. They need to find hobbies and interests outside of their relationships, and make friends with people who will be honest with them.

The person who struggles to commit must learn what rejection truly feels like, so they can stop doing it to others. They must also learn the joys, struggles, highs, and lows of being in a committed relationship, whether it’s romantic or not.

Healing Attachment Trauma

When you find yourself in a relationship with someone who has abandonment issues, you have a delicate role to play in their healing. You are not their healer, nor is the relationship. Your role is to provide healthy companionship and support. We all have some healing to do, and we all need company and compassion as we heal.

When you can see the signs of abandonment issues in your loved ones, you will begin to notice your own issues. Loving someone is like looking in the mirror: you see things you never realized were there, and some things you would rather ignore. This is what keeps us humble, grounded, kind, and intentional. No one is perfect, but we’re not meant to be. We’re all on a journey of getting better and loving better, and the rest we figure out as we go.

Confronting your abandonment issues is hard to do alone, and sometimes even harder to do in a relationship. This is where counseling comes in. It’s easier to examine the issue with someone who is not only trained to help but who doesn’t have an attachment to you beyond being compassionate and professional.

Please consult our online catalog of counselors to find someone suitable, or speak with our reception team, who can help.

item.title: 3 Life Stages When Female Friendships Are Essential
item.description:
Female friendships can be complicated to maintain, tough to build, and even more challenging to restore when there’s a break. It might feel frustrating or pointless to continue putting the work into these relationships. But as you grow and change through life’s seasons, your friends are the ones who sustain you and remind you of your purpose.

Here are five life stages when female friendships aren’t just nice to have but are empowering and essential.

Transitioning into Teen Years with Friendship

This life stage can be fraught with drama, disagreements, and simply changing your mind about so many topics. However, when transitioning from childhood and early adolescence to the teen years, having female friendships for support is integral to emotional and mental health.

When you were 12, 13, or 14, what were you most concerned with? Was it makeup, beauty products, clothing, shoes, or boys? If your answer is yes, you’re in like company. Many young women entering their teen years think about these, too. However, did you know that teen girls today also have deeper, heavier worries on their minds?

Recent research suggests that teen girls are also concerned about long-term decisions, such as where they’ll attend college, what career to pursue, how they’ll earn an income, and family conflict resolution. Just as with adult females, this life stage is one where, without supportive friends, a young teen may find it even more challenging to navigate than it already is.

So, how do teen girls form supportive, healthy female friendships? First, they look to their role models. Many teens learn how to treat friends by the way their parents treat others. If you’re the mother of a teen girl, remember that she’s watching and listening to how you talk to, treat, and talk about your own friends.

Second, pay attention to how your daughter talks about casual friends at school. If one day there’s a breakup, and the next day there’s a hookup between her bestie and her bestie’s boyfriend, it might mean her best girl is prone to drama, mixed signals, or a preoccupation with the things that aren’t lasting. Listening first and asking questions second about your daughter’s friends is one way to tiptoe into discovering what kinds of people she’s around most.

Most teens spend the majority of their time at school, so it’s normal to be lumped together with people you might not ordinarily choose. Much like an office setting where you can’t choose your co-workers, the same goes for school. That’s why asking questions is vital. Not every friend your daughter talks about is going to be her best one, or healthy, and that’s okay. It’s to be expected.

Letting your daughter in on some friendship secrets could help her as she searches for friends who will guard her vulnerability and add joy to her life rather than drama. Secrets you probably didn’t know you had tucked away might include the power of observation.

Talk to your daughter about things like observing how a friend talks about others and paying attention to her discussions around faith or morality. Also, note whether she’s inclined to persevere when something difficult happens or when she’s tasked with a group project. It’s even important to teach her to recognize if a friend asks for help from trustworthy adults if she’s struggling. Remind your daughter to look for good character in her friends.

Another secret you help her learn is to join teams and activities based on interest level and based on who’s involved. As your daughter decides what activities to pursue, remind her that an activity may not be worth pursuing if it means joining a group of girls who go out after a game to party or who talk about others in a demeaning way.

Sometimes teens need to learn the hard way who a good friend is and isn’t. Having an understanding, listening ear is always a gift to her during this season.

Friendships in Young Adulthood

Whether you see young adulthood as 18 or 25, having female friendships can buoy you during these transitional years.

Women face monumental decisions such as where to live, what career to pursue, and how to find a faith community and grow in their spiritual life. This is also the time when many young women start to reflect on their childhood, see some areas for improvement, and desire a closer relationship with family members.

It can be a terrific time to pursue counseling, too. If you or someone you know has been thinking or talking about family relationships or childhood wounds, our offices are widespread and staffed with credentialed, competent counselors, and we’ll match you with the right person to suit your needs.

Female friendships in your early to mid-20s can be tough to maintain when so many women are in life transitions. Whether they’re getting married, starting a career, pursuing a post-graduate degree, or having children, women during this life stage may find it hard to be consistent with their old friends and carve out time to make new ones.

Some tips we want to remind young women are that they have a unique personality and gifts to share. Old ways of connecting, like community service, are sometimes overlooked unless you’re heavily plugged into a service-oriented church.

Aside from contributing your time or talents to a cause you believe in, community service is also a wonderful way to form female friendships. Look for causes that matter to you, and you’ll likely find others who have at least one interest in common.

Another way to find or maintain female friendships at this stage is to develop a creative communication method that works most of the time. This isn’t the time to wish your friend a casual “let’s keep in touch” or “let’s get together next month.” If you want to maintain friendships, you’ll have to be direct, intentional, targeted, decisive, and a little creative.

Use apps like Marco Polo or WhatsApp to help you stay in touch with regular video chat exchanges or life update check-ins. Arrange to talk regularly and create a Zoom call where you can agree on a set time period (not to cut each other off but to respect each other’s time and commitments during this life stage).

Think about a friend who is getting married. Her life is changing radically, so she might not be able to predict what her everyday life will look like after marriage. But give her a month or so, and then try to connect at a time that works for her. You can mutually decide how often you want to call or text to check in and how you plan to maintain your friendship in a season where your lives may not align.

Consider all that you do have in common and don’t write her off simply because her life stage will shift. She’s going to need a friend who knew her before her marriage and can remind her who she is on tough days. And you’ll benefit from getting insider info on what it’s like to be married. Everything she goes through while adjusting is something you can file away and learn from in the future.

Friendships When Your Children Are Grown and on Their Own

You may be newly empty-nested or empty-nested for a decade, but somewhere in this life stage, friends are going to come in handy. Here’s why.

Being suddenly empty can shock our systems. For some of us, it’s an easy transition at first. But then, after years of watching our adult children make choices on career, life, and love, we may encounter a time when our needs fade into the background of their thriving, busy lives.

It’s not that you aren’t happy that they are doing so well (you are!), but when their lives get chaotic, fruitful, stressful, and full, it’s common for them to forget to include a parent in their world. That’s if you’re close geographically; it’s even harder when you live far away.

Friends can be the balm to your loneliness and feeling left out because they can help you find new interests, explore ideas you’ve never considered before, or take risks that you once would have balked at. Now you have the time, energy, and financial resources to pursue them.

They can also listen when you feel left out, give you a kick in the pants when you need to be reminded you’re not a victim, and help you learn how to be vulnerable when it’s the last thing you want to be.

If you’re newly empty-nested, a friend who stays beside you regardless of her life stage is a treasure. She may not be able to relate to what you are going through, but she can mirror what she sees in you and echo what she hears you say. Having female friendships where we’re heard, seen, and known can carry you through just about anything.

You can carry someone else through this life stage, too. Here’s how:

  • Call and invite her for coffee or a walk, even if she says no too many times. (Don’t give up.)
  • Show up at her house with a to-go coffee from her favorite cafe, chicken salad and croissants, or a puzzle you can work on together. It reminds her that she still has needs and interests outside of her children.
  • Engage in her stories about her children, even if you’ve heard similar ones. Listening to her is a way of holding space for her grief, joy, pain, and the immense transition she’s going through right now.
  • Ask her to try something new with you, somewhere new together. Trying something you’ve never done together builds camaraderie in a way that old hobbies can’t. You’ll probably have to be brave together, and it’ll elicit some laughs, giving your grieving friend a place to escape for a little while.
  • Encourage your friend to attend counseling. Even if it’s just a few sessions, seeing a counselor during seasons of transition can provide her with healthy tools and mindset shifts.

To schedule an appointment with me or one of the other counselors in our online directory, contact our reception team today at Vancouver Christian Counseling in Washington state.

item.title: Ways Your Helicopter Mom Affected Your Mental Health
item.description:
Sometimes it is the best intentions that cause the most enduring damage. That certainly is the case for anyone who grew up being parented by a helicopter mom. This style of invasive parenting is not a recent phenomenon.

The term dates back to a phrase from a book on parenting that was published in 1969, where a teen describes his controlling mother as always hovering over him in the background. In the decades since 1990, the idea of helicopter parenting has become increasingly discussed, with many proudly self-identifying as helicopter parents.

When compared to neglectful parents, helicopter moms appear as attentive, engaged, and involved in their children’s lives. In truth, however, the average helicopter mom is causing layers of psychological and emotional damage to her children, often without meaning to.

It’s a complicated thing to realize as an adult that your parent did more harm than good. Some people are forever affected by their helicopter mom. It is only when they begin to confront their past and make changes in their present that they can undo some of the damage that was done.

The Defining Aspects of a Helicopter Mom

It’s important to accurately identify what a helicopter mom is and determine what sets them apart from a healthy, attentive parent. Currently, there are many parents who proudly wear the label of helicopter parent simply because they are intentional, involved, and engaged in their child’s life. There are, however, several important differences between nurturing parents and helicopter parents.

During infancy and early childhood, the idea of being a helicopter parent is acceptable, to a point. There are many ways a baby or a toddler can injure themselves, and many situations that require a parent to monitor their child carefully.

At a certain age, it is important to lengthen the strings that connect you to your child. You must allow them space to grow, make mistakes, and learn to make good choices. A helicopter parent does not adapt or adjust their parenting style as their child grows.

The helicopter mom remains overly involved in all aspects of their child’s life, often into teen years and sometimes adulthood. Under her anxious glare, the child cannot make any decisions without first consulting her.

They cannot develop individuality or form their own opinions. It is often difficult to perform vital but ordinary tasks, such as cooking, cleaning, or performing basic hygiene. The helicopter mom has inserted herself into so many aspects of her child’s life that she is the sun around which her child’s life orbits.

The Helicopter Mom: Intention Versus Impact

As the saying goes, the path to destruction is paved with good intentions. There are multiple reasons why someone becomes a controlling, invasive, anxious parent, but it is almost always done out of concern and with good intentions. As an adult sorting through the damage that was done in your childhood from a helicopter parent, it’s important to distinguish your parents’ intention from the impact they have had on your life.

For example, your helicopter mom might have tried to shield you from pain, disappointment, and failure. These are important aspects of life, though, and you will only develop and mature if you learn to face them.

If you were never permitted to fail, you will feel guilty and ashamed each time you do. If you were protected from discomfort, you would feel helpless in every challenge. If you were never allowed to make a choice, even the wrong one, you will never have confidence in your ability to move forward in life or adapt to difficult situations.

Without meaning to, helicopter moms ensure their kids enter adulthood as dependent, anxious, confused people, who often feel guilty, ashamed, or resentful, without even knowing where those feelings come from.

The Dark Turn

In some cases, helicopter parenting produces much darker results. Helicopter parents are micromanagers who constantly communicate that they mistrust their children. To a teen who is desperate for some space to develop their own identity, or an adult who craves the feeling of independence, this is insulting, frustrating, and stifling.

Sometimes the only way to fully experience freedom is rebellion. They might lash out in anger, build boundaries so high that the relationship becomes strained, or resort to burning bridges. When you strip back the layers of helicopter parenting, you expose anxiety, distrust, and a need for control. Treating someone this way, even under the guise of love, will result in nothing good.

At best, the child will grow into an insecure, fearful adult with no confidence or coping skills and a constant need for validation. At worst, they will be resentful, damaged, trapped, and eager to find a way out. This will come as a shock to the micromanaging parent, who has likely convinced themselves that everything they did came from the best intentions.

Finding Healing and Wholeness

Adults who were impacted by a helicopter mom have a difficult path ahead of them as they attempt to resolve their trauma from the past. Many people manage to maintain a close relationship with their controlling parent, despite realizing the damage that was done. Even when they can trace their current issues back to their experiences growing up, pinning all the blame on their parents doesn’t help them find peace.

The great trick of healing from trauma caused by a helicopter parent is in learning to give space to feeling mixed emotions. You can be both grateful for your mother’s involvement and concern in your life, while also being frustrated by her dominance and control.

You can love her, but also reduce her impact in your life by setting up boundaries. You can be angry about the way she instilled anxiety and fear into your life, but recognize that she has the same struggles without anyone helping her.

One of the most important things you can do for your healing is to identify specific behaviors that were shaped or inspired by your helicopter mom. Whether it is a feeling of general helplessness, guilt, anxiety, a fear of failure, or a constant need for validation, identify each one individually and call it out.

Acknowledge it is part of your psyche, that it impacts your life, and note where it came from. Expect to feel anxious in this process because you are confronting things that your nervous system has been trained to avoid.

An important part of this process is identifying your mother’s voice in your head. The helicopter mom voice often says things like, “Ask me before doing this,” or “You’ll only mess this up if you try it yourself.” If you were taught that failure is scary and that you can’t be trusted to try new things, you already know what you need to do. Hear that voice in your head, tell it to hush, and do it anyway.

Freedom

Helicopter parents position themselves to be the single most important resource in their child’s life, regardless of how old or in what stage of life their child is. This does not always come from a place of narcissism or self-importance, though sometimes it does. At the core of this parenting style is anxiety and fear disguised as love and concern.

Your helicopter mom might have reduced your confidence, heightened your anxiety, and diminished your identity. There is always time to address these things and start living your life free from the overbearing influence of a micromanaging parent. It is a difficult road to walk, and there might be a few fraught confrontations to initiate, but you have what it takes to do this.

You might need support as you venture forth in confronting your past. We suggest meeting with a counselor with whom you can share your journey. We hope that you can find someone suitable on our online catalog, or someone from our reception team can help you.
